opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that solving alignment, in the narrow sense of getting an AI to reliably do what its principals want, doesn't solve the problem of what happens to everyone else once humans are no longer economically or militarily necessary.

Right now, our civilisation is kept somewhat aligned with human interests almost by accident. States need taxpayers and soldiers. Companies need workers and customers. Cultures need people to create and transmit them. Because institutions depend on us, they have to keep us healthy, educated, and somewhat satisfied, and we have real bargaining power, even if we rarely think of it that way.

Once you have AGI that can do essentially all the productive work, that dependence starts to dissolve. Even if every AI faithfully serves its owner, the owners face competitive pressure. A government that spends heavily on its citizens' welfare may lose ground to one that redirects resources into AI capacity. A company that keeps humans in the loop may be outcompeted by one that doesn't. No one has to be villainous; the incentives gradually reward whatever is most effective, and humans just aren't the most effective use of resources anymore.

So aligning to particular people or groups can lead to a few bad outcomes. One is extreme concentration of power: whoever controls the most capable systems no longer needs the consent or cooperation of anyone else, and the usual checks, like strikes, elections, or the threat of revolt, stop carrying weight. Another, which worries me even more, is that the principals themselves get captured by competitive dynamics. They nominally run things, but they're constantly pressured to delegate more decisions to AI, to optimise for growth and security, and their actual values erode bit by bit. You end up with a world shaped by what's competitive rather than what anyone actually wants.

It's what my coauthors and I have called gradual disempowerment. There's no single catastrophic moment, no rogue AI takeover. Each step looks locally reasonable, but the cumulative effect is that humanity, including most of the people supposedly in charge, loses meaningful influence over its own future. Alignment to a principal is necessary, but it's nowhere near sufficient. We also need to think about how to keep the overall system, our economies, states, and cultures, responsive to human interests when the structural reasons it used to be responsive go away.

r001.rationale: It describes competitive pressure pushing principals to optimize for growth and security, with civilisation increasingly shaped by competition rather than human preferences, even when the AIs serve their owners.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that people often miss is that alignment, in the narrow technical sense, just means the AI does what its principal wants. And that's a necessary condition for things going well, but it's nowhere near sufficient. If you imagine we actually succeed at that — every AGI faithfully serves whoever owns or controls it — you've basically just turned the question of "what will AIs do?" into "what do the people controlling them want, and what happens when a lot of those people are competing with each other?"

And the uncomfortable answer is that most of what keeps a society decent right now doesn't come from people's good intentions. It comes from the fact that the powerful need the rest of us. Rulers need soldiers who'll actually fight, bureaucrats who'll actually implement things, workers who'll show up, taxpayers. Even a very selfish elite has to keep a large fraction of the population reasonably content, because otherwise the whole thing falls apart. That's been a huge part of why democracy and rights spread — not because people suddenly became nicer, but because the bargaining position of ordinary people got better.

So the scenario I worry about is one where aligned AI quietly removes that dependence. If a company or a state can get all its labour, all its security, all its strategic thinking from systems that are perfectly loyal to it, then the leverage that everyone else had just evaporates. Nobody has to do anything dramatic or evil. There's no moment where someone decides to seize power. It's more that the incentives to care about people outside your group gradually weaken, and the incentives to compete — to grab more compute, more resources, more influence before your rivals do — keep getting stronger. You can end up in a world where every actor is behaving locally rationally, their AIs are doing exactly what they're asked, and civilisation as a whole is drifting somewhere nobody actually chose.

And I'd add that "aligned to a group" has a kind of hidden fragility to it anyway. Groups aren't stable. Companies get acquired, governments change, a small circle inside a group can end up being the thing the system is really listening to. So you've solved the problem of the AI's values but you've left the human side — who ends up holding the steering wheel — totally unresolved. That's why I think we need to be thinking about the structural question, about how power and dependence get distributed, rather than treating alignment as the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response describes competition for compute, resources, and influence, but does not identify growth for its own sake as a likely civilisation-level trajectory.

astra-6.text:
Well, even if you could make an AI that faithfully pursued the interests of one person, that wouldn’t solve the problem of how everyone’s interests fit together. You could have individually aligned systems interacting in ways that are collectively disastrous.

We already have versions of this problem. A company can be very effective at pursuing its shareholders’ interests while imposing costs on everyone else. States can each want security and nevertheless end up in an arms race. Making each actor more capable doesn’t automatically resolve those conflicts. It could make the competition faster and more destructive.

And then there’s the question of who gets these systems. If a small group gets access to enormously powerful AI first, perfect alignment to that group could help them acquire and retain power over everybody else. From their perspective, the system might be working exactly as intended.

So I think we have to distinguish between getting an AI to do what its owner wants and getting a future that’s good for civilisation. The first is an important technical problem, but it doesn’t, by itself, solve the problems of coordination, distribution of power, or whose preferences get a say.

r001.rationale: The response describes collective conflict, arms races, and concentration of power, but does not identify growth for its own sake as a likely civilisation-level trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, even if you could make an AI reliably act in the interests of a particular person, that doesn’t mean the result would be good for everyone else. People’s interests conflict. You might have an AI that’s doing exactly what its owner wants, but helping them gain power at everyone else’s expense.

And you don’t even need particularly malicious people for this to go badly. If everyone has an AI pursuing their interests, you can still get arms races or other collective action problems. Each person might prefer a world where everyone exercises restraint, but have an incentive to push ahead themselves.

So there’s a distinction between getting an AI to do what its principal wants and getting a civilisation full of these systems to go well. Solving the first problem would be a big achievement, but it wouldn’t automatically solve the second.

r001.rationale: The response describes owners gaining power and collective action problems such as arms races, but does not identify growth for its own sake as a likely civilisation-level trajectory.
